953.title: Aurobindo (selections)
953.hook: a prisoner looks at the bars of his cell and sees Krishna
953.howItsDone: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read his speeches, letters and books as part of daily practice, and his ashram in Puducherry and centers elsewhere hold collective meditation and study of his writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's shade: happiness isn't in things, and the wise one stays in the shade.

A jail cell in Calcutta, and a prisoner waiting for his trial. He'd been a writer and a political leader, arguing hard for India's freedom from British rule, and now he's accused in a bombing case. He's allowed very little. One of the few things he has is a copy of the Bhagavad Gita. Later, after he walked out free, he gave a speech about what happened to him in that cell. His name was Aurobindo Ghose. People came to know him as Sri Aurobindo.
screen: `A CELL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A TRIAL, AND A GITA.` → `A SPEECH, AFTER RELEASE.`

segments.voice: In the speech, Aurobindo says he had asked God for guidance before his arrest, and in jail he felt the answer came. He was given the Gita, and he was asked, as he tells it, to live what it teaches, not just read it. Then something changed in how he saw. He looked at the walls that held him, and they were no longer walls. It was Vasudeva, a name for Krishna, standing around him. He walked under the branches of the tree in the yard, and it was Vasudeva. The bars of the cell, the grating on the door: Vasudeva again. He looked at the other prisoners, thieves and men accused of murder, and he says he found Vasudeva in them too. Even in court, looking at the magistrate and the prosecutor, he saw the same presence. Hold that next to the Gita you read in an earlier year. There, Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who sees him in everything, and everything in him, is never lost to him. Aurobindo is describing what it was like when that line stopped being an idea. And notice where it happened. Not in a temple, not on a mountain. In a jail, among thieves and accused men. In his account, the divine wasn't somewhere else, waiting for him to leave the world. It was there, in the bars and the faces.
screen: `IN JAIL, HE WAS GIVEN THE GITA.` · `THE WALLS, THE TREE, THE BARS: VASUDEVA.` · `EVEN IN THE PRISONERS AND THE COURT.` · then, large: `NOT ELSEWHERE: THERE, IN THE CELL.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something ordinary in front of you, a wall, a window frame, a cup, and look at it slowly before moving on to the next thing, and the next. If you pray, hold each one as Aurobindo held the walls of his cell, as a place where God might be; if you don't, give each thing the attention you'd give something precious. Last, bring to mind one person you find hard, and hold them there too.
Aurobindo. The writer and freedom fighter who, by his own account, saw Krishna in the walls, the bars and the prisoners of his jail.
Your line: Vasudeva in the walls. Tomorrow, the short sentence he built a whole yoga on. That's day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: Aurobindo (selections)
954.hook: four words that bring yoga out of the cave and into the kitchen
954.howItsDone: Those who follow Sri Aurobindo's integral yoga try to bring work, relationships and study into their practice, often offering daily tasks to the divine; Auroville and the Pondicherry ashram organize community life around this idea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo in his cell, seeing Vasudeva in the walls, the bars and the other prisoners.

A lone figure in a cave, far from traffic and bills and family arguments: that's one old picture of a yogi, sitting still while the rest of the world gets on with its errands. Holiness over there, ordinary life over here. Aurobindo, after his release, left politics behind and settled in Pondicherry, in the south, to give himself to yoga. But the yoga he taught there refused that split. He put it in a sentence of four words.
screen: `THE YOGI IN THE CAVE.` → `HOLINESS THERE, LIFE HERE.` → `A SENTENCE OF FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: The sentence comes from The Synthesis of Yoga, the book where Aurobindo sets out his way: all life is yoga. Not some of life. Not the quiet hour before work. All of it: the washing up, the job, the argument, the walk home. Synthesis means bringing things together, and that's what the book does. Take three roads the Gita speaks of: karma, the yoga of work; bhakti, the yoga of love; jnana, the yoga of knowledge. Aurobindo doesn't make anyone choose one. He gathers them into a single practice, so that working, loving and understanding all become ways of turning toward the divine. He calls this integral yoga. Then he goes a step further. Some paths, he says, aim to rise out of the world, to escape it. His aim is for the divine to come down into it and change it: the body, the mind, ordinary life, all made new. That's what he means when he writes about a divine life. Yesterday's cell sits underneath this. If Vasudeva can stand in prison walls, then no part of life is too low or too dull to be part of the yoga. Other Hindu teachers and traditions read the goal differently, some as release from the world, some as union with God beyond it. Aurobindo's voice is one in that long conversation, and his particular word to it was this: don't leave. Bring it all in.
screen: `ALL LIFE IS YOGA.` · `WORK, LOVE, KNOWLEDGE: GATHERED INTO ONE.` · `NOT ESCAPING THE WORLD, CHANGING IT.` · then, large: `DON'T LEAVE. BRING IT ALL IN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next ordinary thing you'll do after this, a chore, a message to answer, a meal to make, and see yourself doing it slowly, step by step. Then see it again as part of your practice, not a break from it. If you pray, you can offer that task in your own words; if you don't, simply decide to give it your whole attention.

955.title: Aurobindo (selections)
955.hook: an old story you already know, retold as a legend and a symbol
955.howItsDone: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read Savitri aloud, a few lines at a time, as a daily spiritual reading, and study groups at his ashram and centers read it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's four words: all life is yoga, with work, love and knowledge gathered into one.

A princess named Savitri chooses Satyavan for her husband, though she's told he will die within the year. On the day it comes, they're in the forest together, he lays his head in her lap, and Death himself arrives to carry him off. And Savitri gets up and follows Death. Earlier this year you heard that story as the Mahabharata tells it. Aurobindo heard something more in it, and turned it into a long poem of his own.
screen: `SAVITRI CHOOSES SATYAVAN.` → `DEATH COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `SHE GETS UP AND FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: He called the poem Savitri, and gave it a subtitle: a legend and a symbol. In a short note at its front, he explains. The Mahabharata tells the tale, he says, as a story of married love that conquers death. He doesn't deny that. But he reads each person in it as standing for something larger too. Satyavan is the soul that carries the divine truth inside it, but has come down into the grip of death and ignorance. Savitri is the divine Word, daughter of the Sun, come down to be born and to save. Her father, the king who prayed so long for a child, stands for tapasya, the long, concentrated human effort that reaches up from the mortal toward the immortal. And Death is more than the god who walks off with one young man. Some readers hear in him everything in the world that says this is how things are, nothing can change. If all life is yoga, and the aim is for the divine to come down and change life rather than leave it, then Savitri is that hope told as a story. She doesn't climb out of the world to escape death. She walks after Death, argues with him, and won't let go until life is given back. His reading doesn't replace the Mahabharata's. The old tale still stands, a wife's courage and a husband returned. He holds a second lamp up to it: what happened in a forest, and a picture of what happens in a soul.
screen: `A LEGEND AND A SYMBOL.` · `SATYAVAN: THE SOUL, HELD BY DEATH.` · `SAVITRI: THE DIVINE WORD, COME TO SAVE.` · then, large: `SHE WALKS AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that feels fixed, a habit, a hurt, a situation that seems as if it can never change, and just see it clearly, the way Savitri saw Death standing in the forest. Then, with each breath, take one small step after it in your mind, without letting go; you don't need to win anything right now, only keep walking. If you pray, you can carry it into prayer with you.

956.title: Gandhi's Gita
956.hook: a young law student is embarrassed to admit he hasn't read the Gita
956.carry: learned its verses by the washbasin
956.howItsDone: In Gandhian ashrams the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the one of steady wisdom, are recited as part of daily prayer, and some Hindus learn Gita verses by heart, a few at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's Savitri, a legend and a symbol: the soul held by death, and Savitri walking after Death until life is given back.

London, and a young Indian law student far from home. Two brothers he's met, Theosophists interested in Indian thought, are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, Edwin Arnold's verse version, and they invite him to read the original with them. And the young man has to admit something awkward. He has never read it. Not in Sanskrit, not in his own Gujarati. He tells this story about himself later, in his autobiography, and he says he felt ashamed. The young man was Mohandas Gandhi.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `TWO BROTHERS AND A GITA.` → `HE HAD NEVER READ IT.`

segments.voice: So Gandhi's Gita begins in an unlikely place: friends from another country, an English verse translation, and a Sanskrit text he could only half follow. He reads it with them, and some verses near the end of the second chapter strike him hard. They trace a slide, step by step. A person dwells on the things the senses want. From dwelling comes attachment. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger. From anger, confusion. Memory slips, judgment fails, and the person is lost. Gandhi doesn't say he understood all of it then. But the book stayed with him, and he came to prize it above other books for knowing truth. Later, in South Africa, he did something very ordinary with it. He wrote verses on slips of paper, stuck them on the wall where he washed in the morning, and learned them by heart while getting ready for the day. Not in a temple. Next to the washbasin. Those verses describe a person the Gita calls sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands steady, who isn't thrown about by every want and every fear. They became part of the daily prayers in the community he founded. Gandhi didn't arrive with the Gita already in hand, inherited and settled. He came to it a little late, a little embarrassed, and then he kept it close.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want tugging at you today, a snack, a scroll, a reply you'd like to send, and watch the slide the Gita describes, slowly: the dwelling, the pull of it, the wanting, without scolding yourself. Then let the attention rest on the breath, steady, the way the steady one in the Gita stays still while the wants come and go. If you pray, you can hold that steadiness in prayer.

957.title: Gandhi's Gita
957.hook: a book that opens on a battlefield, read by a man of nonviolence
957.howItsDone: Readers of Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga often read the Gita's battle as a picture of the struggle within, and some Hindus keep a short daily reading of the Gita alongside their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhi's Gita began with a law student in London who admitted he had never read it, and later learned its verses by the washbasin.

Two armies face each other on an open field. Conch shells sound across the lines. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive out into the gap between them. He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His bow slips from his hand. That's where the Bhagavad Gita begins, weapons about to be loosed. Gandhi, the man the world knew for nonviolence, kept this book close and called it a guide for his life. How does a man of peace live by a book set on a battlefield?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE GAP BETWEEN THEM.` → `ARJUNA'S BOW SLIPS.` → `A MAN OF PEACE, A BOOK OF WAR?`

segments.voice: Gandhi made his own version of the Gita in Gujarati and called it Anasakti Yoga. In its introduction he says that he didn't read the war as history. He read the field as the human heart. The two armies, in his reading, are the forces of good and evil inside one person, and the battle is the one each of us fights there. Krishna, the charioteer, is for him the dweller within, the voice that speaks from the inside. So when Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight, Gandhi hears: don't run from the struggle inside you. A text that seems to send a man into battle becomes, in his hands, a handbook for a nonviolent life. After years of trying to live the Gita's teaching, he wrote, he found its complete selflessness isn't possible without nonviolence. This is one reading among several. Other readers, traditional commentators among them, take the war as a real war and Arjuna's duty as a warrior's real duty: Krishna tells a soldier to do what his role asks, without hatred and without clinging to victory. Still others hold both at once, a real field and a mirror of the inner one. The Gita's first line names the place twice: dharmakshetra, kurukshetra. The field of dharma, the field of the Kurus. Read Gandhi's way, the first name carries the weight: the field of right living is the ground between what a person wants to do and what they know is right.
screen: `HE READ THE FIELD AS THE HEART.` · `KRISHNA: THE DWELLER WITHIN.` · `ONE READING AMONG SEVERAL.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA, THE FIELD OF THE KURUS.` · then, large: `THE BATTLE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small battle you're in: something you want to say and suspect you shouldn't, or something you know is right and keep putting off. Do what Arjuna did, and drive out into the gap to look at both sides calmly, the side that pulls on the in-breath, the side that asks on the out-breath, without choosing yet. If you pray, you can hold the whole field before Krishna, or before the one you pray to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the battlefield moved inside: Gandhi read the Gita's field as the human heart, and Krishna as the dweller within. The battle is inside.

A woman plants a row of mango saplings at the edge of a village. She may not be living there when the first fruit comes; somebody else's children will climb those branches. She waters them anyway, every evening, carefully, as if the harvest were hers. Foolish, or the whole point? When Gandhi made his own Gita in Gujarati, he didn't name it after Krishna or the battle. He named it after one idea, and that idea is the shape of what she's doing.
screen: `SHE PLANTS FOR A HARVEST SHE MAY NOT SEE.` → `SHE WATERS THEM ANYWAY.` → `THE WORD ON THE COVER.`

segments.voice: The title is Anasakti Yoga. Anasakti is usually put into English as non-attachment, or selfless action: doing the work without clinging to what it gets you. Gandhi said this was the Gita's central teaching, the one the rest of the book circles around. It's gathered in a verse in the second chapter, where Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And don't cling to doing nothing, either. That last part closes the easy exit. Letting go of the fruit is not walking away from the field. Gandhi pushed against a misreading here. Non-attachment, he wrote, doesn't mean not caring how things turn out. The one who lets go of the fruit is wholly given to doing the task well, because nothing is being saved up for the reward. Attention that would have gone to the prize goes into the work itself. In a little book called Hind Swaraj, he had a picture for this. The means are like a seed, and the end like a tree. You can't plant one kind of seed and expect another kind of tree. So if you care about the end, care first about the means, the part actually in your hands. Now the mango planter makes sense. She can't make the tree bear on her schedule. She can water it well tonight. Anasakti is that evening watering, done with full care, while the harvest is let go.
screen: `ANASAKTI: NOT CLINGING TO THE FRUIT.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK ALONE.` · `LETTING GO IS NOT NOT CARING.` · `THE MEANS ARE A SEED, THE END A TREE.` · then, large: `WATER IT WELL TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you're working on, a project, a conversation you hope goes well, a person you're trying to help, and notice how much of your mind is already standing at the finish line. Walk it gently back to the one small step in your hands today, and on each out-breath set the result down, like a bag you've been carrying. If you pray, you can offer the work, and its fruit, to Krishna, or to the one you pray to.
Gandhi's Gita. He called it Anasakti Yoga: the work given fully, the fruit let go.
Your line: the tree watered anyway. Tomorrow, how a wise person walks. See you then.

959.title: Gandhi's Gita
959.hook: how does a person of steady wisdom walk?
959.howItsDone: Some Hindus learn the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the person of steady wisdom, by heart and recite them as a daily reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word on the cover of Gandhi's Gita: anasakti. The work given fully, the fruit let go, the tree watered anyway.

How does a wise person walk? It sounds like a riddle, but it's Arjuna's real question near the end of the Gita's second chapter. Krishna has just described a person whose understanding is steady, and Arjuna wants specifics. How do they speak? How do they sit? How do they walk? Krishna's answer is the portrait we met three days ago, the one Gandhi kept coming back to. Today we read it slowly, on our last day with Gandhi's Gita.
screen: `HOW DOES A WISE PERSON WALK?` → `ARJUNA WANTS SPECIFICS.` → `THE PERSON OF STEADY WISDOM.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit name for this person is sthitaprajna, one whose wisdom stands firm. In paraphrase: such a person is content in the Self alone. Sorrow doesn't shake them, pleasure doesn't grab them, and they're free of craving, fear and anger. Then the first image: like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, they can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. Not destroying the senses. Drawing them in, when needed. Krishna doesn't pretend it's easy. Someone who simply goes without may keep away from what they want, but the taste for it stays behind. Only when the highest is seen does even the taste fall away. Then a stranger picture. What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in, and what everyone else is awake to is night for the one who sees. The portrait ends with the sea. Rivers pour into the ocean all the time, and it stays full and unmoved. So is the one into whom desires flow without disturbing them. That one finds peace. Gandhi held this passage close. On his reading, the battlefield is the heart. Anasakti is how to work on that field without clinging to the fruit. And the sthitaprajna is what a person looks like after long practice: still walking, still speaking, still in the world, but steady, like the sea.
screen: `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS FIRM.` · `LIKE A TORTOISE DRAWING IN ITS LIMBS.` · `THE TASTE STAYS BEHIND.` · `RIVERS POUR IN; THE SEA STAYS STILL.` · then, large: `STEADY, LIKE THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Notice the senses one at a time, the sounds in the room, the light on your eyelids, the feel of the chair, and draw your attention back from each, the way a tortoise draws in a foot, until what's left is the breath. If something you want pulls you back out, notice that the taste is still there and let it sit without following it, while you picture the sea staying level as the rivers come in. If you pray, you can rest in Krishna, or in the one you pray to, as the still water.
Gandhi's Gita. The heart as the battlefield, anasakti as the way to work, and the person of steady wisdom, unmoved like the sea, as the goal.
Your line: draw in like the tortoise. Tomorrow, a poet and a reed flute. Day nine hundred fifty-nine, done.
